timeAndLogRules: Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, session schedules, travel timing, event boards, and deadlines. Use Belavadös dates second for lore records, temple calendars, journals, festivals, and immersion. A Belavadös astronomical year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long, and those solar days are distributed evenly across the Earth year for table play.

For sky calculations, use solar progress rather than the named civil date. The civil calendar still has 330 named dates arranged as eleven 30-date months, while the 0.15 solar-day correction is spread through the year as a tiny clock drift. There is no bonus day or frozen end-period for moons, planets, tides, omens, or the Star-River.
Write sky events Earth-first, then Belavadös-second: Earth Month Day, Year, local time with UTC label / Belavadös month date, weekday, Belavadös clock, solar-day progress, moon phase, and sky note.

Settlement and province sky notes may include the settlement UTC when the observing site differs from the province primary UTC. Province summaries should show only one or two Earth-style UTC labels, while exact settlement exports can store the UTC chosen by longitude.
skySetting: The analysis assumes a view from approximately 30° N latitude. At 30° N, stars above about +60° declination are circumpolar, while stars below about -60° declination never rise.

The sky looks dark, dense, and sharply structured. With no electric skyglow, the Star-River of Belavadös would have been a major visible feature rather than a faint haze. Bright planets, bright stars, both moons, and future named sky patterns can serve as seasonal markers, navigation guides, calendar anchors, and story-bearing landmarks.

The Star-River of Belavadös is the luminous band of unresolved stars and dark rifts crossing the night sky. In summer evenings, it would stretch through the southern gate-and-serpent sectors and climb toward the northern seasonal markers. In winter evenings, it would run near the Bronze Bull region, becoming paler but still visible under dry, dark conditions.

From desert-edge skyfields, the Star-River would not have appeared as a smooth strip. It would have looked mottled, braided, and broken by dark channels. The brightest warm-season section would have been low-to-mid in the southern sky; the higher northern section would have served as a nightly path for visual navigation.

nebulaFields.name: Âhufej
nebulaFields.layer_structure: Foreground soot lanes (900 ly), dense emission nursery (1,380 ly), red-brown rear cloud (5,800 ly)
nebulaFields.texture_components: Dense newborn stellar nursery with glowing hydrogen chambers. Rose tones arise from ionized hydrogen, gold from embedded young stars illuminating dust grains, while smoke-violet regions form where cooler molecular gas mingles with shadowed dust curtains. Texture resembles folded velvet mixed with branching smoke channels. Numerous protostars, Bok globules, and accretion knots are embedded throughout.

nebulaFields.name: Dus‘idu
nebulaFields.layer_structure: Silver strand foreground (1,100 ly), supernova shell (2,100 ly), violet mutation veil (6,200 ly)
nebulaFields.texture_components: Extremely filamentary remnant structure. Cyan and jade hues indicate oxygen-rich shock fronts while white regions mark compressed gas where multiple shock waves intersect. Texture appears as torn silk, braided tendrils, and lace-like membranes. Contains expanding ejecta sheets, ionized oxygen filaments, sulfur traces, and high-energy particle fronts.

nebulaFields.name: Ềdizfu
nebulaFields.layer_structure: Foreground sparks (1,800 ly), storm sheet (4,200 ly), primary rift flower (5,600 ly), violet dust rear layer (7,900 ly)
nebulaFields.texture_components: Vast petal-shaped dark nebula carved through a glowing emission field. Crimson and magenta petals surround blue-black voids where dense molecular dust blocks starlight. Texture resembles layered flower petals made of smoke and velvet. Contains cold molecular clouds, active collapse zones, dark filaments, and bright ionization ridges outlining the rift edges.

nebulaFields.name: Juçdimx
nebulaFields.layer_structure: Front ash layer (2,000 ly), reflective dust basin (3,400 ly), curse smoke (5,100 ly), under-road shadow (10,300 ly)
nebulaFields.texture_components: A highly reflective dust field illuminated by nearby blue stars. Silver and pearl regions arise from light scattering by fine silicate particles. Texture resembles finished frost, drifting fog banks, and layered mirror-glass sheets. Contains reflective silicate dust, carbonaceous smoke clouds, and fragmented molecular lanes.

nebulaFields.name: Jadd-Jisud
nebulaFields.layer_structure: Metal-blue shell (2,200 ly), green shell (4,800 ly), primary red-amber shell cluster (8,900 ly), lost-key echo layer (9,600 ly)
nebulaFields.texture_components: Collection of overlapping planetary-nebula remnants. Amber and red shells arise from hydrogen and nitrogen emissions, while charcoal gaps reveal exhausted central cavities. Texture appears as stacked bubbles, fractured onion skins, and cracked glass spheres. Components include dying stellar cores, expanding gas shells, metallic ion clouds, and dusty ejecta rings.

nebulaFields.name: Horundar
nebulaFields.layer_structure: Tide mist (1,600 ly), reservoir core (1,900 ly), reef sheet (3,900 ly), blackwater wall (8,700 ly)
nebulaFields.texture_components: Diffuse cloud filled with icy cometary material. White and ice-blue coloration results from starlight reflecting from frozen dust and microscopic ice crystals. Texture resembles sea fog, frost plumes, and subcombined currents. Rich in volatile compounds, comet embryos, crystalline ice grains, and reflective dust sheets.

nebulaFields.name: Wougen
nebulaFields.layer_structure: Blue foreground haze (1,200 ly), star-forming core (2,850 ly), mirror sheet (3,600 ly), rose backwash (6,300 ly)
nebulaFields.texture_components: Massive molecular cloud actively producing stellar clusters. Green-gold regions arise from mixed oxygen and dust reflection, cream tones from warm embedded stars. Texture resembles billowing cream-colored thunderheads crossed by turquoise rivers. Components include molecular hydrogen reservoirs, stellar nurseries, evaporating gas pillars, and young cluster cavities.

nebulaFields.name: Ŝiowoei
nebulaFields.layer_structure: Silver foreground threads (2,000 ly), central spiral coil (4,200 ly), violet rear dust (7,900 ly)
nebulaFields.texture_components: A rotating spiral dust formation resembling a galactic whirlpool. Dark blue channels mark denser dust lanes while silver highlights indicate reflected starlight. Texture resembles braided ribbons, hurricane bands, and coiled smoke. Contains spiral molecular filaments, reflective silicates, and embedded star embryos tracing the coil arms.

layouts.skykeeperReading: A maze of horn, stone, burden, and watchfire. Giants, minotaurs, cavern guides, and winter cattlefolk read this figure as the gate of endurance. In the Age of Open Gods, vows of strength were sworn under it before mountain crossings and before entering deep stone. At its height, Anubaldir was believed to weigh every road against the body that dared to walk it.

layouts.name: The Star-River
layouts.skykeeperReading: The mottled river of stars and dark rifts crossing the night. Sailors, caravan leaders, moon-priests, burial clerks, and desert-edge farmers all used it as a road above roads. It is not smooth: it braids, breaks, foams, and darkens like floodwater under two moons. Its bright southern depth is watched for omens; its winter branch runs pale and cold through the high air.

phaseFormulae: 3. belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this value for moon phases, planetary positions, tides, constellations, seasons, and sky omens.
4. belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this value only for the named Belavadös month and date.
5. Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.

These month names are used for date labels only. A moon, wandering world, tide, season, or sky omen should still be calculated from belSolarDayProgress so the sky remains smooth across the full Earth year.

The lunar system is nested: the larger moon orbits the world, while the smaller moonlet orbits the larger moon and is carried along with it. This creates paired lunar calendars, small bead-like crossings, and a subtle secondary tidal pulse. For Earth sessions, both lunar positions are calculated from belSolarDayProgress, not from the civil month and date.

A representative high-era observing night can be generated by first calculating belSolarDayProgress from the Earth date and local observing time, then placing Chandratecu-Seleneš and Mictlindra-Nannara along their 19.20-day and 2.02-day cycles. A sample scene may place the paired lunar system near RA 06h 15m and Dec +18° to +19°, close to the northern cold-season field and high enough for easy viewing from 30° N.

Dense newborn stellar nursery with glowing hydrogen chambers. Rose tones arise from ionized hydrogen, gold from embedded young stars illuminating dust grains, while smoke-violet regions form where cooler molecular gas mingles with shadowed dust curtains. Texture resembles folded velvet mixed with branching smoke channels. Numerous protostars, Bok globules, and accretion knots are embedded throughout.

Extremely filamentary remnant structure. Cyan and jade hues indicate oxygen-rich shock fronts while white regions mark compressed gas where multiple shock waves intersect. Texture appears as torn silk, braided tendrils, and lace-like membranes. Contains expanding ejecta sheets, ionized oxygen filaments, sulfur traces, and high-energy particle fronts.

A highly reflective dust field illuminated by nearby blue stars. Silver and pearl regions arise from light scattering by fine silicate particles. Collection of overlapping planetary-nebula remnants. Amber and red shells arise from hydrogen and nitrogen emissions, while charcoal gaps reveal exhausted central cavities. Texture appears as stacked bubbles, fractured onion skins, and cracked glass spheres. Components include dying stellar cores, expanding gas shells, metallic ion clouds, and dusty ejecta rings.
